strengths: The task and dataset provide the main basis for weak acceptance. Jointly segmenting sounding instances, preserving their identities, and identifying their active periods is a meaningful extension of binary and semantic audio-visual segmentation, with clear relevance to multimodal video understanding.

AVISeg represents a substantial annotation contribution: 926 videos averaging 61.4 seconds, 94,074 masks, and 26 categories across four scenarios. Including silent frames and 59.16% multi-source frames creates useful challenges beyond the shorter clips in existing AVS benchmarks.

The baseline has supporting evidence independent of the proposed FSLA metric. With the reported common ResNet-50 backbone and training schedule, AVISM achieves 61.73 HOTA and 40.57 mAP, compared with COMBO's 57.39/37.84 and VITA's 57.48/36.25 (Table 2). Improvements therefore extend to established tracking and segmentation measures.

The architecture is a sensible adaptation of object-token association to audio-visual processing. Table 4 supports the incremental benefit of both fusion stages, while Tables 5–6 examine window size and pretraining. The supplementary qualitative comparisons and explicit same-category failure cases help characterize the method's capabilities.
weaknesses: FSLA is not reproducibly specified. Algorithm 1 credits silent ground-truth frames without checking predictions, never uses the supplied category labels, lacks an explicit check that every instance and the object count are correct, and initializes counters outside the threshold loop without resetting them. Its frame-count aggregation also differs from the class averaging described in Sections 3.2 and 9.3. These inconsistencies materially undermine the new metric's specification, although they do not establish that the implementation producing the tables contains the same errors.

The large-model conclusions exceed what the adaptations establish. Sections 11.1–11.2 merge same-category masks into one identity, Section 11.4 treats each category as one instance, and the Sam4AVS adaptation selects only the top-1 audio class. These restrictions structurally prevent some required outputs. Table 3 demonstrates limitations of the selected pipelines, but cannot cleanly attribute their poor instance-level performance to the underlying large models.

The strongest temporal-localization claims need more direct support. Section 5.3 describes a video query shared across frames being applied to image-only pixel embeddings; it does not clearly explain how instantaneous audio activity controls each frame's final mask. The aggregate fusion ablation establishes usefulness, but no audio-timing control or quantitative analysis of same-category activity transitions establishes the claimed disambiguation mechanism. Window-capacity measurements alone also do not demonstrate long-range accuracy.

Documentation of the benchmark's reliability and reproducibility is incomplete. Section 4 reports repeated manual refinement but gives no quantitative annotation audit or detailed protocol for adjudicating ambiguous overlapping sounds and maintaining identities through silent intervals. Source-level deduplication and split-disjointness checks are not documented, and the manuscript supplies no explicit dataset or implementation access location. These omissions limit independent assessment and reuse of the paper's principal contribution.
